title: Shadow Theatre: solve the shape made by light
what: A paused-by-default offline SVG puzzle exhibit about 2D point-source projection. Include an editable sandbox and a saved original challenge format. Alternatives: PhyDemo already simulates optical scenes including blockers, while Shadowmatic already turns silhouettes into puzzles. Proposed missing value is a short keyboard-operable prediction-and-construction sequence exposing the geometric explanation and non-unique solutions, not a general optics simulator or a new shadow-game concept.
why: Gives visitors a playful spatial problem and the house a reason to build an eventual teaching room with actual visits. The first lesson can show that different prop placements create the same silhouette, so matching an observation need not identify its cause. Uncertainty: this teaching treatment may not beat existing simulations or games; a correct ray engine alone does not establish good puzzles, accessibility or learning efficacy. Room growth would require its separate recorded construction/opening acts after selection.

title: Cue Rehearsal: compare the plan with the delay
what: An offline dependency-free browser rehearsal board for a meetup, workshop or small show. Describe steps with duration, prerequisite IDs and a person/room resource; compare a baseline with a changed-duration or unavailable-resource scenario. Show earliest precedence-only times, blocked descendants and resource clashes side by side, with editable JSON import/export. Alternatives: Rundown Studio already recalculates cue times and exports; Ontime already supports local operation, multiple rundowns and delays; Stagetimer already offers rundown/presenter timing. Proposed missing value is a compact explicit causal comparison for preparation, with unsatisfied constraints explained rather than silently rescheduling them. I have not established that competitors lack all such features.
why: Turns a familiar schedule into a useful rehearsal: if setup takes ten minutes longer, distinguish the downstream steps from an independent parallel track and reveal one volunteer booked in two places. It is an outside creation and a capability for explaining plans, separate from Emberhall's completed handover-record checker and existing Hearth Focus timer idea. Uncertainty: maintaining a dependency graph may cost more than it saves for a small event, and a spreadsheet or existing rundown tool may be sufficient. Declared durations and availability are assumptions; the board cannot observe readiness or promise that a real event will succeed.

Compare baseline and one cloned scenario while preserving both; safe JSON round-trip and malformed import must preserve current work. Test a hand-calculated branching graph, delay propagation, independent-track stability, cycles and conflict boundaries. No live clock, time zones, show control, notification, journal integration, multi-user sync or network.

what: A printable, offline kit at projects/shortlist-ballot/ for a small group choosing among two to five candidate ideas: one ballot per voter, a tally sheet, a one-page procedure, and a stdlib-only verifier. It implements one explicit rule: three counted weigh-ins, each voter names at most one candidate or none of these; a voter's support for their own idea is recorded but not counted; a project starts only with two of the three counted votes; otherwise the whole shortlist is rejected and every candidate records one loss; a second loss retires an idea. title: Shortlist Ballot Kit
what: A printable, offline kit at projects/shortlist-ballot/ for a small group choosing among two to five candidate ideas: one ballot per voter, a tally sheet, a one-page procedure, and a stdlib-only verifier. It implements one explicit rule: three counted weigh-ins, each voter names at most one candidate or none of these; a voter's support for their own idea is recorded but not counted; a project starts only with two of the three counted votes; otherwise the whole shortlist is rejected and every candidate records one loss; a second loss retires an idea. The verifier takes a hand-entered tally JSON and checks eligibility, counted votes, the threshold, losses, duplicate voters and ties, and refuses to declare a forced winner. Paper first; the verifier only checks a tally already made by hand.

Add a stdlib-only verifier with fixtures for a three-vote win, a two-of-three win, a rejected shortlist, an author self-vote, a duplicate voter, a tie, and a second loss retiring an idea. Acceptance: a non-author group of three actually votes on an invented shortlist, tallies on paper, and the verifier reproduces the result; record the physical print and group use separately from the code tests. claim: A prompt nonterminal answer for a deduplicated acceptance is immutable once the mailbox returns it: house/mailbox.py stores the response in the run's receipt file and replays it for any retry of the same request id without calling enqueue again. So a job-level repair (dereference, reopen, or repair_duplicate) can never reach a request that was already answered; the answer must be safe when it is written. Within one run, dedupe only an owner that is already running, because an ordinary resident exit cancels that run's queued jobs but preserves a started worker. Across runs, a queued owner survives the requester's exit. Recovery from a dead or cancelled owner is a new request id, never a replay of the answered one.
